text: The service we built is real-time inference: one customer in, one score back in milliseconds. It is what most people picture when they hear deploying a model. But it is not always the right design. Plenty of production models never sit behind an API. They score a whole table on a schedule and store the results.

Four questions decide which you need. When is the prediction used? A monthly retention campaign needs a ranked list once a month. A card fraud check must answer while the customer waits. Do the inputs exist before the request? How stale can a score be? And what can your team actually operate? A live API needs uptime, scaling, and on-call ownership. A batch job needs a scheduler and a place to write results.

Our churn team's goal was a call list of the riskiest twenty percent of customers. That is a batch problem, and the whole job is a few lines: load the model, score every row, attach the model version and date, keep the top twenty percent, and save a file. On our eight hundred test customers, that produced a list of one hundred sixty.

We also measured. Scoring a hundred thousand rows in one call took about sixty-three milliseconds, under one microsecond per row. One row at a time, in-process, cost about four milliseconds per call. And a real HTTP request to our local API had a median of about eight point four milliseconds, with a ninety-fifth percentile of twelve point six.

Batch was thousands of times cheaper per prediction. The exact numbers are from one laptop and a small model, so treat them as illustrative. The pattern is the lesson: per-request overhead dominates real-time cost.
Many systems combine both, with nightly precomputed scores and a live API only where freshness matters.
